extracted.intended_audience: authors, reviewers, editors, and journal staff of Royal Society journals
extracted.subtask_short: Royal Society journal peer review policy
extracted.subtask_description: Editorial and peer-review standards and procedures for submission, review, correction, and post-publication debate across Royal Society journals. Covers anonymity models, reviewer/co-reviewer expectations, appeals, corrections/retractions, name-change policy, and handling integrity concerns.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial independence
rubrics_metrics.description: The content of Royal Society journals is entirely independent of the Society’s views on any scientific or policy issues; the editor’s decision is final and will not be influenced or compromised by the Society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors' decisions are final and must be made without external influence from the Society.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review anonymity model
rubrics_metrics.description: Most papers are peer reviewed in a single-anonymized fashion (author names are not concealed, but referee names are); Notes and Records and Proceedings B are double-anonymized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors and reviewers should expect the stated anonymity model for the specific journal; journal webpages provide details for each title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bias mitigation in peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Measures to ensure fairness and minimise bias include striving to have a diverse representation on editorial boards, encouraging board members to select reviewers from a diverse pool (including author suggestions), regularly reminding board members/reviewers/staff to be aware of unconscious biases, and working with other publishers to collect anonymised diversity data.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial boards are expected to implement these measures when selecting reviewers and making decisions to reduce systemic bias in peer review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer of peer-reviewed preprints
rubrics_metrics.description: Open Biology accepts transfer of peer-reviewed preprints directly from Review Commons into the editorial workflow, where they are assessed for publication without restarting peer review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors can transfer reviews via Review Commons when submitting to journals that accept such transfers (check journal-specific guidance).

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication of peer-review information (transparent peer review)
rubrics_metrics.description: For Royal Society Open Science, Open Biology and Proceedings B, publication of peer review information (anonymous by default unless the reviewer signs their report) is mandatory. For Proceedings A and Biology Letters, authors are offered the option to publish peer review information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should expect journal-specific policies on publishing peer review reports; anonymity defaults and opt-in/mandatory status vary by title.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality of referee reports and correspondence
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless published with the article, referee reports and other correspondence relating to a paper must remain confidential and should not be shared or made publicly available. Confidential discussions remain confidential unless explicit consent is given by all parties or exceptional circumstances apply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reviewers and authors must treat peer review correspondence as confidential during and after the review process unless all parties consent to disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prohibition on referees using generative AI with manuscript details
rubrics_metrics.description: Referees inputting manuscript details into generative AI tools is prohibited.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The policy rationale: AI tools provide no guarantee of where data are being sent, saved, viewed, or used in the future; reviewers must not disclose manuscript content to such tools.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guest-editor-managed review for Philosophical Transactions
rubrics_metrics.description: For submissions to the Philosophical Transactions journals, the guest editor of the issue manages the review process and is encouraged to seek at least two referees for each paper.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guest editors should aim for at least two referees to ensure adequate peer review for issue papers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor/board member recusal from decisions on own work
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors or board members are never involved in editorial decisions about their own work; such papers may be referred to other editors or the editor-in-chief.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Where an editor/board member is an author, another independent editor should handle the manuscript to avoid conflicts of interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on edits to reviewer reports
rubrics_metrics.description: Edits to reviews are kept to an absolute minimum and address only issues of tone, language, and deviations from journal policy and reviewer guidelines; edits will not change the meaning or intention of the review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editorial staff may make minimal editorial changes to ensure reports comply with policies and are professionally worded, but substantive content must remain unchanged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy on abusive behaviour
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society does not tolerate abusive behaviour or correspondence towards staff, academic editors, authors or reviewers. Any author who engages in abusive behaviour will have their paper immediately withdrawn from consideration; subsequent submissions will be at the editor's discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors must maintain professional conduct in all correspondence; abusive conduct has immediate and strong consequences for submissions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-reviewing definition and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: A co-reviewer is a researcher (often early career) or technician who reviews a manuscript together with a more senior (invited) reviewer. The senior reviewer is limited to one appropriately qualified co-reviewer per review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Co-reviewing is supported as a learning experience but should be limited (one co-reviewer per senior reviewer) and agreed upon by both parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-review disclosure and accountability
rubrics_metrics.description: The review process is strictly confidential. To provide accountability and appropriate credit, the name and status (e.g. PhD student) of the co-reviewer should be disclosed on submission of the review. The senior reviewer is the main point of contact and ultimately accountable; senior reviewer and co-reviewer should agree on the wording; confidentiality and competing interests rules apply to both.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When submitting a review with a co-reviewer, disclose the co-reviewer's identity and status; ensure both agree on review content and adhere to confidentiality and conflict-of-interest policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Co-review name disclosure when peer-review info published
rubrics_metrics.description: For journals where peer review information is published, the senior reviewer may disclose their name to obtain credit; there is also the opportunity to include the co-reviewer’s name provided they have given consent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consent is required from co-reviewers before publishing their names; senior reviewers can opt to receive credit as per journal practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to appeal editorial decisions
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors have a right to appeal editorial decisions. The author should submit the grounds for their appeal to the editorial office, addressed to the editor. Authors are discouraged from directly contacting editorial board members and editors with appeals. Following an appeal, all editorial decisions are final.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Appeals must be submitted formally to the editorial office; direct contact with board members is discouraged; after the appeal process, decisions are final.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editors mediate exchanges during peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors will mediate all exchanges between authors and referees during the peer review process (prior to publication). If agreement cannot be reached, editors may invite comments from additional referees if appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors should route responses and disputes through the editor; editors can seek additional independent referee input to resolve disagreements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expression of concern usage
rubrics_metrics.description: An expression of concern is used to make readers aware that the journal has concerns about the accuracy of an article and that it is currently being investigated or evaluated; normally it will be in effect during the decision-making process only.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expressions of concern are temporary notices while investigations proceed and inform readers that issues are under review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correction (corrigendum/erratum) criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A correction is normally used when a small portion of an otherwise reliable publication proves to be misleading. Errors which require correction include: anything that changes data or the scientific meaning; anything contained in metadata elements (e.g., title, authors, affiliations, funding info); any other error where it is imperative that all readers and downstream vendors have the updated version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corrections should be issued when errors materially affect data/meaning or metadata, and must be applied so downstream services receive the updated information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Retraction criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: A retraction is a notification of invalid results and/or conclusions and will be considered if: editors have clear evidence that findings are unreliable (because of misconduct such as data fabrication/falsification or honest error like miscalculation), the findings have been previously published elsewhere without proper cross-referencing (redundant publication), it constitutes plagiarism, or it reports unethical research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retraction is appropriate for fundamentally invalid or unethical work; journals should document clear evidence and follow established procedures when retracting.

rubrics_metrics.name: Addendum and editor's note purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: An addendum can be used to provide additional information or clarification and focuses on what needs changing or clarifying; it is not a forum for debate. An editor’s note is a less formal communication to draw attention to a particular aspect of an article when the above article types are not appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use addenda for factual clarifications or additions; use editor’s notes for informal notices that don't fit correction/retraction/addendum categories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Format and discoverability of notices (correction/expression/retraction/addendum)
rubrics_metrics.description: Notices are written so readers can identify and understand the correction/retraction/editor's concerns. Notices have their own DOI but are linked electronically with the original publication; the original article remains online with the notice linked. They are published so indexing/abstracting services can identify and link corrections and retractions, published at the end of the latest issue and appear on the table of contents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Notices must be clearly written, assigned DOIs, linked to the original article, made discoverable for indexing, and published in the journal issue TOC.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and marking of retractions
rubrics_metrics.description: A retraction must be authored by one of the following: the author, the author's legal counsel, the author's sponsoring institution, the editorial office or the editor of the journal. Retracted articles remain on the journal website but are clearly marked as retracted (with updated metadata and Crossmark record) and the PDF version carries a watermark on every page.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retractions must be traceable to an authorized authoring party and full electronic marking and metadata updates must be made to clearly indicate retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Participation in CrossMark and version tracking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Royal Society participates in CrossMark to provide a standard way for readers to locate the current version of content; clicking the logo tells the status of a document and may give additional publication record information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should use CrossMark to signal current document status and link to publication history/updates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Raising and processing concerns about research integrity
rubrics_metrics.description: Concerns can be raised by any party (authors, researchers, readers, institutions), anonymously or publicly; confidentiality when requested will be respected. Allegations are brought to the Editor-in-Chief, who acknowledges receipt and asks for evidence; allegations are shared with authors and they are asked for their response while respecting confidentiality requests. The Editor-in-Chief should follow COPE flowcharts. Investigations vary in complexity; aim is to determine research integrity/reliability, not the integrity of individuals. Investigations may involve committees, other journals, legal representatives, authors’ institutions; publisher communications may be involved. If investigation is lengthy, an expression of concern may be issued. Before action, editor's findings should be reviewed with the publishing team to ensure consistent approach and best practice. Final decision is communicated to authors and, if necessary, other relevant bodies; retraction notice posted and published.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow COPE guidance, gather evidence, give authors opportunity to respond, involve relevant expertise, communicate decisions transparently, and issue interim notices when needed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Author name-change policy after publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors may change their name (for reasons such as marriage, divorce, religion, gender identity). The Royal Society will facilitate changes to author names, email addresses, biography photos, pronouns, and other identifiers. These changes will be made directly to the article PDF and HTML; metadata will be re-sent to indexing services though replacement on their platforms cannot be enforced. The DOI remains the same. The Royal Society will retain an original version in a secure environment, not public. Authors should contact the editorial office to request changes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals will update public article files and attempt to update metadata with indexing services while preserving DOI and keeping an archived original for records; authors must request changes via the editorial office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open criticism and debate policy
rubrics_metrics.description: Academic debate and constructive criticism of research is encouraged. Authors do not have a right to veto unfavourable comments about their work, but may choose not to respond. No referee comment or published correspondence may contain a personal attack on any of the authors. Criticism of the work (not the researcher) is encouraged and editors should edit (or reject) personal or offensive statements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Comments should focus on work and evidence, avoid personal attacks; editors may moderate or reject comments that are personal or offensive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment and reply submission and review rules
rubrics_metrics.description: A comment highlights an oversight or proposes an opposing view, often providing corrections or new analyses. If factual errors affecting the record are identified, a corrigendum/erratum may be published instead. Comments are not for addressing ethical issues (use COPE). A comment can be proposed by any reader within three months of online publication of the initial article and will be published at the editor's discretion. The comment is peer-reviewed, usually by a referee from the original article and another impartial referee, and is shared with the corresponding author. If accepted, it is held to allow a reply from the original authors. The reply will also be peer-reviewed (if it passes triage). Comment and reply is normally limited to one round.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submit comments within three months; expect peer review; editors may allow one round of comment and reply; ethical issues should follow COPE procedures rather than comments.
